intro: When a sentence **starts** with a negative or limiting word, such as *never, rarely, hardly, not only, only when*, we use **question word order** (auxiliary + subject): ***Never have I** seen such a beautiful view.*
This is called **inversion**. It's formal and emphatic, and it's common in writing, speeches and storytelling.

rows: I have **never** seen such a view.
**Never have I** seen such a view.
**Rarely do we** see talent like this.
He was late **and** he forgot the tickets.
**Not only was he** late, but he also forgot the tickets.
I realised **only when** I got home.
**Only when** I got home **did I** realise.

blocks.md: If there is no auxiliary, add **do / does / did**: *We rarely see… → Rarely **do** we see…* With *be*, just put *be* first: *Not only **was he** late…*

items: ***Never / Rarely / Seldom*** *(+ present perfect or present simple):* *Seldom **has** he been so angry.*

***Hardly / Scarcely… when*** and ***No sooner… than*** *(one thing immediately after another, usually past perfect):* *Hardly **had** we arrived **when** it started to rain. No sooner **had** I sat down **than** the phone rang.*
***Not only… but (also)***: *Not only **does** she speak French, **but** she also speaks Arabic.*
***Only when / Only after / Only then / Not until***: the inversion is in the **main** clause: *Not until the end **did** we find out the truth.*
***Under no circumstances / On no account / At no time / In no way***: *Under no circumstances **should** you open this door.*
***Little*** (= not at all): *Little **did** I know that my life was about to change.*

blocks.md: *No sooner* goes with **than**; *hardly / scarcely* go with **when**. Don't mix them.

items.text: **Never have I** felt so proud.
**Rarely do** we get snow in April.
**Seldom has** the city looked so beautiful.
**Hardly had** the match started **when** it began to rain.
**No sooner had** she left **than** he arrived.
**Not only is** the hotel cheap, **but** it's also very comfortable.
**Only after** the meeting **did I** understand the problem.
**Not until** I got home **did I** notice the missing wallet.
**On no account must** you share your password.
**Little did** they know that we were watching.

mistakes.wrong: Never I have seen such a mess.
mistakes.right: Never have I seen such a mess.
mistakes.why: After a negative adverbial at the start: auxiliary + subject.

mistakes.wrong: Rarely we go to the cinema.
mistakes.right: Rarely do we go to the cinema.
mistakes.why: No auxiliary in the normal sentence: add do / does / did.

mistakes.wrong: No sooner had I arrived when it rained.
mistakes.right: No sooner had I arrived than it rained.
mistakes.why: No sooner goes with than.

mistakes.wrong: Only when I got home I realised.
mistakes.right: Only when I got home did I realise.
mistakes.why: With only when, the inversion is in the main clause.

mistakes.wrong: Not only he is clever, but he's also kind.
mistakes.right: Not only is he clever, but he's also kind.
mistakes.why: Not only at the start: inversion.

mistakes.wrong: Under no circumstances you should leave.
mistakes.right: Under no circumstances should you leave.
mistakes.why: Modal + subject after a negative adverbial.

items.prompt: Never ___ such a beautiful sunset.
items.explanation: Never at the start: **have I** seen.

items.prompt: No sooner had we sat down ___ the phone rang.
Hardly ___ arrived when it started to rain.
items.explanation: Hardly… when + past perfect inversion: **had we** arrived.

items.prompt: Not only ___ late, but he also forgot the tickets.
Rarely ___ such talent in a young player.
items.explanation: No auxiliary, so add *do*: Rarely **do we see**.

items.prompt: Only when I got home ___ that I had lost my wallet.
items.explanation: Inversion in the main clause: **did I realise**.

items.prompt: Under no circumstances ___ the door to strangers.
Little ___ that his life was about to change.
items.explanation: Little (= not at all) + inversion: **did he know**.

items.prompt: Not until the end of the film ___ who the killer was.
items.explanation: Not until… + inversion in the main clause: **did we find out**.

items.prompt: Seldom ___ he been so angry.
items.explanation: Present perfect inversion: Seldom **has** he been…

items.prompt: At no time ___ the passengers in danger.
items.explanation: With *be*: At no time **were** the passengers in danger.

items.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Only after the meeting I understood the problem.
Only after the meeting understood I the problem.
Only after the meeting did I understand the problem.
Only after the meeting I did understand the problem.

items.prompt: Hardly had she left ___ he arrived.
No sooner ___ the house than I realised I'd forgotten my keys.
items.explanation: No sooner + past perfect inversion: **had I left**.

items.prompt: Not only does she speak French, ___ she also speaks Arabic.
On no account ___ leave your bags unattended.
items.explanation: Modal + subject: **must you**. (*On no account* is already negative.)

topics.h1: Cleft Sentences (It was... that, What I need is...)
intro: A **cleft sentence** splits one idea into two parts to **emphasise** one of them: *Tom broke the window. → **It was Tom who** broke the window.* (Tom, not someone else.)
There are two main types: **it-clefts** and **wh-clefts**.

sections.h2: It-clefts: It is / was + focus + that / who

blocks.md: Put the part you want to emphasise after *It is / It was*, then add *that* (or *who* for people):

rows: **It was Tom who** broke the window.
**It was the window that** Tom broke.
**It was in 2015 that** we moved to Canada.
I realised only when I got home.
**It was only when** I got home **that** I realised.

blocks.md: *It* + singular *be* stays the same with plural focus: ***It was** my parents who paid.* We often use it to correct: *It's not the money I care about, **it's** the people.*
Start with a *what* clause, then *is / was*, then the focus: *I need a holiday. → **What I need is** a holiday.*

items: For an action, use *do*: ***What I did was** (to) call the manager.*
For an event: ***What happened was (that)** the car broke down.*
Similar patterns: ***All I want is** a cup of tea. **The thing that** surprised me was… **The reason why** I left was… **The place where** we met was…*

blocks.md: The verb after the *what* clause is usually singular: *What we need **is** more time.* Don't add *it*: *What I like **is**…* (not *What I like it is*).

items.text: **It was my sister who** told me the news.
**It's** the noise **that** I can't stand, not the heat.
**It was** in Paris **that** they first met.
**What I need is** a long holiday.
**What annoys me is** people who talk during films.
**What we did was** book a taxi.
**What happened was that** we got lost.
**All I want is** some peace and quiet.
**The reason why** I'm late **is** that the train was cancelled.
**The thing that** surprised me most **was** the price.

mistakes.wrong: It was my brother which called.
mistakes.right: It was my brother who called.
mistakes.why: For people, use who or that.

mistakes.wrong: What I need it is a holiday.
mistakes.right: What I need is a holiday.
mistakes.why: Don't add it after the what clause.

mistakes.wrong: That I want is a new job.
mistakes.right: What I want is a new job.
mistakes.why: Wh-cleft starts with what.

mistakes.wrong: What I did was I called the police.
mistakes.right: What I did was (to) call the police.
mistakes.why: After what I did was, use the (to-)infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: It were the students who complained.
mistakes.right: It was the students who complained.
mistakes.why: Use singular It is / It was.

mistakes.wrong: The reason because I left was the hours.
mistakes.right: The reason why I left was the hours.
mistakes.why: The reason why (or the reason that).

items.prompt: ___ I need is a long holiday.

___ annoys me is people who talk during films.

items.explanation: Correcting with an it-cleft: **It's** the people…

items.prompt: The reason ___ I left was the long working hours.

Choose the correct sentence.
options: What I like about her it is her honesty.

options: It was the window that Tom broke.

intro: A **participle clause** is a short way to give information without a full clause with a subject and conjunction: *As she opened the door, she saw… → **Opening the door**, she saw…*
They are common in writing and make sentences more concise.

rows: active; at the same time, or a reason
**Feeling** tired, I went to bed early. (= Because I felt tired)
**Built** in 1889, the tower is now a symbol of Paris. (= It was built)
active; one action finished before another
**Having been warned** about the traffic, we left early.

blocks.md: Negative: put **not** first: ***Not knowing** what to say, I stayed silent.*
A participle can replace a relative clause: *The woman **who is sitting** next to me → The woman **sitting** next to me. The people **who were invited** → The people **invited**.*
Use *being* + -ed for a passive action in progress: *The bridge **being built** now will be the longest in the country.*

We can keep the conjunction for clarity: ***Before leaving**, turn off the lights. **While living** in Japan, I learned a lot. **After graduating**, he moved abroad. **When asked**, she refused to comment.*

sections.h2: The subject must be the same

blocks.md: The participle clause and the main clause normally share the **same subject**. Otherwise the sentence is wrong or funny (a *dangling participle*):

items.text: Walking home, the rain started.
**Walking home**, I got caught in the rain.
**Realising** it was late, we took a taxi.
**Woken** by the noise, the baby started crying.
**Having left** his keys at home, he couldn't get in.
**Not knowing** the area, we got lost.
Anyone **wishing** to join should contact the secretary.
Most of the people **invited** to the party were old friends.
The letter, **written** in pencil, was hard to read.
**Before leaving** the room, please turn off the lights.
**Abandoned** by his friends, he felt very lonely.
**Having been told** the news, she called her parents.

mistakes.wrong: Walking along the beach, the sun was setting.
mistakes.right: Walking along the beach, we watched the sun set.
mistakes.why: The participle and the main clause need the same subject.

mistakes.wrong: Building in 1889, the tower is famous.
mistakes.right: Built in 1889, the tower is famous.
mistakes.why: Passive meaning: past participle.

mistakes.wrong: Knowing not the answer, I said nothing.
mistakes.right: Not knowing the answer, I said nothing.
mistakes.why: Not goes before the participle.

mistakes.wrong: Having finish the report, she left.
mistakes.right: Having finished the report, she left.
mistakes.why: Having + past participle.

mistakes.wrong: The man sits next to me was reading.
mistakes.right: The man sitting next to me was reading.
mistakes.why: Reduced relative clause: -ing.

mistakes.wrong: Before to leave, lock the door.
mistakes.right: Before leaving, lock the door.
mistakes.why: Conjunction + -ing.

items.prompt: ___ in 1889, the Eiffel Tower is now a symbol of France.
The woman ___ next to me on the train was reading a fascinating book.
items.explanation: Reduced relative clause, active: **sitting** (= who was sitting).

items.prompt: ___ the door, she realised someone had been in the house.
items.explanation: Active, at the same time: **Opening** (= as she opened).

items.prompt: Most of the people ___ to the party were old friends.
items.explanation: Passive reduced relative: **invited** (= who were invited).

items.prompt: ___ his keys at home, he couldn't get into the flat.
Not ___ what to say, I stayed silent.
___ by the noise, the baby started crying.

items.prompt: ___ all the exercises, she checked her answers.
While ___ in Japan, I learned a lot about the culture.

intro: Natural English avoids repeating words. We either **replace** them with a short word (**substitution**) or **leave them out** (**ellipsis**):
*I don't like this jacket. Can I see the blue **one**?* (substitution) *I can't swim, but my sister **can**.* (ellipsis: *can swim*)

rows: These shoes are too small. Do you have bigger **ones**?
She speaks French better than I **do**.
He was asked to leave, and he **did so** at once.
Is the shop open? – I'm afraid **not**.

blocks.md: *So / not* are common after *think, hope, expect, suppose, guess, be afraid*: *I hope **so**. I hope **not**. I expect **so**.*
With *think, expect, suppose*, the usual negative is *I don't think **so*** (more natural than *I think not*). With *hope* and *be afraid*, use *not*: *I hope **not**. I'm afraid **not**.*

items: After an auxiliary or modal: *I haven't finished, but Sara **has**. Will you help? – Yes, I **will**.*
After *to* (keep the *to*): *Would you like to come? – I'd love **to**. I didn't want to go, but I had **to**.*
After *and, but, or*, when the subject or verb is the same: *She washed the dishes and (she) dried them.*
In short answers and replies: *Who wants cake? – I **do**!*

items.text: I'd like a coffee. Would you like **one**?
The red apples are sweeter than the green **ones**.
Nobody works harder than she **does**.
Are you coming tonight? – I hope **so**.
Is it going to rain? – I hope **not**.
I don't think **so**.
I've never been to Asia, but my brother **has**.
Do you want to come? – I'd love **to**, but I'm busy.
Applicants who wish to apply should **do so** by Friday.
She said she'd call, and she **did**.

mistakes.wrong: I don't think it.
mistakes.right: I don't think so.
mistakes.why: Use so to replace a clause.

mistakes.wrong: I hope no.
mistakes.right: I hope not.
mistakes.why: Negative substitution: not.

mistakes.wrong: I'd love.
mistakes.right: I'd love to.
mistakes.why: Keep to when the verb is left out.

mistakes.wrong: These are the old ones shoes.
mistakes.right: These are the old ones.
mistakes.why: Ones replaces the noun; don't use both.

mistakes.wrong: She can't come, but her husband can come it.
mistakes.right: She can't come, but her husband can.
mistakes.why: After the auxiliary, leave out the repeated words.

mistakes.wrong: I like this cheese. Do you like one?
mistakes.right: Do you like it?
mistakes.why: One replaces a countable noun; for the same specific thing, use it.

topics.h1: Passive Reporting Structures (It is said that..., He is thought to...)
intro: In news and formal writing, we often report what people in general say, think or believe without saying who: *People say that he is rich. → **It is said that** he is rich. / He **is said to be** rich.*
Common verbs: *say, think, believe, know, report, expect, consider, claim, allege, estimate, suspect*.

rows: **It is believed that** the thieves left the country.
The thieves **are believed to have left** the country.

blocks.md: With **there**: *There **are said to be** over a million people in the square.*

rows: He is said **to be** very rich.
She is reported **to be recording** a new album.
Shakespeare is thought **to have written** it in 1599.
He is believed **to have been living** abroad.

blocks.md: The reporting verb can be past too: *She **was reported to have left** the hospital.*

items.text: **It is said that** the castle is haunted.
The castle **is said to be** haunted.
**It is expected that** prices will rise.
The new bridge **is expected to open** in 2028.
The singer **is reported to be recording** a new album.
The painting **is estimated to be worth** $5 million.
The suspect **is alleged to have stolen** the money.
**It is known that** the drug has side effects.
He **is considered to be** one of the best players in the world.
There **are thought to be** around 3,000 tigers left in the wild.

mistakes.wrong: He is said that he is rich.
mistakes.right: It is said that he is rich. / He is said to be rich.
mistakes.why: Don't mix the two patterns.

mistakes.wrong: It says that the company will close.
mistakes.right: It is said that the company will close.
mistakes.why: Use the passive: it is said.

mistakes.wrong: He is believed to leave yesterday.
mistakes.right: He is believed to have left yesterday.
mistakes.why: Earlier action: to have + past participle.

mistakes.wrong: She is reported being in hospital.
mistakes.right: She is reported to be in hospital.
mistakes.why: Use the to-infinitive.

mistakes.wrong: There is said to be many problems.
mistakes.right: There are said to be many problems.
mistakes.why: Plural noun: there are.

___ that eating carrots improves your eyesight.

items.prompt: There ___ to be over a million people at the protest.
items.explanation: There + plural noun: There **were said** to be…

items.prompt: Shakespeare is thought ___ this play in 1599.

options: The man is believed that he is dangerous.

The man is believed to be dangerous.
items.explanation: Subject + passive + to-infinitive: **The man is believed to be dangerous.**

items.explanation: An action before the report: **to have left**.

topics.h1: Inverted Conditionals (Had I known, Should you need...)
intro: In formal English, we can leave out *if* and **invert** the subject and the auxiliary: *If I had known → **Had I known**. If you need help → **Should you need** help.*
This works with three words only: **should, were** and **had**.

rows: If you need any help, call me.
**Should you need** any help, call me.
If I were you, I'd accept.
If I had known, I'd have come.

blocks.md: Don't use *Will, Would, Did* or *Was* in this structure. Only **Should, Were, Had**.
Put **not** after the subject, and don't use contractions: ***Had I not** seen it…* (not *Hadn't I seen it*). ***Should you not** wish to continue…*
Fixed phrases: ***Were it not for** your help, …* (= If it weren't for) and ***Had it not been for** your help, …* (= If it hadn't been for).

items.text: **Should you have** any questions, don't hesitate to ask.
**Should the problem continue**, contact our support team.
**Were I** in your position, I would accept the offer.
**Were I to win** the lottery, I'd buy a house by the sea.
**Had we left** earlier, we wouldn't have missed the train.
**Had she accepted** the job, she would have moved to New York.
**Had I not seen** it, I wouldn't have believed it.
**Were it not for** the rain, we could have a picnic.
**Had it not been for** your help, we would have failed.
**Had I known** you were coming, I'd have cooked dinner.

mistakes.wrong: Hadn't I known, I wouldn't have gone.
mistakes.right: Had I not known, I wouldn't have gone.
mistakes.why: No contraction: Had I not…

mistakes.wrong: Would you need help, call me.
mistakes.right: Should you need help, call me.
mistakes.why: Use should, not would.

mistakes.wrong: Was I you, I'd apologise.
mistakes.right: Were I you, I'd apologise.
mistakes.why: Use were for all persons.

mistakes.wrong: Had I know, I would have helped.
mistakes.right: Had I known, I would have helped.
mistakes.why: Had + past participle.

mistakes.wrong: If had I known, I would have come.
mistakes.right: Had I known, I would have come.
mistakes.why: Leave out if when you invert.

mistakes.wrong: Were it not of your help, we'd fail.
mistakes.right: Were it not for your help, we'd fail.
mistakes.why: Fixed phrase: Were it not for.

___ you need any help, please call me.
___ I in your position, I would accept the offer.

topics.h1: The Unreal Past (It's time we left, I'd rather you didn't)
intro: After certain expressions, we use a **past tense** to talk about the **present or future**. The past tense shows that the situation is **unreal**, imagined or wanted: *It's time we **went** home.* (We haven't gone yet.)
To talk about an unreal **past**, use the **past perfect**: *She looked as if she **had seen** a ghost.*

rows: He talks as if he **knew** everything.

blocks.md: In formal English, *were* is used for all persons: *He acts as if he **were** the boss.* (*was* is common in speech).

sections.h2: Would rather: same subject or different subject?

blocks.md: **Same subject**: *would rather* + **base form**: *I'd rather **stay** at home.*
**Different subject**: *would rather* + subject + **past**: *I'd rather **you stayed** at home.* For the past, use the past perfect: *I'd rather you **hadn't told** her.*
You may hear the base form after a different subject in American English (*I'd rather you call me*). The past form is correct everywhere.
*It's time **to go*** (general) and *It's time **we went*** (it's a bit late) both work. *It's **high / about** time* adds criticism: *It's about time you **got** a job!*
For *wish* and *if only*, see [Wish and If Only](/blog/grammar/wish-if-only/).

items.text: It's late. It's time we **went** home.
It's high time the government **did** something about pollution.
I'd rather you **didn't** tell anyone.
I'd rather **stay** in tonight.
Would you rather I **called** you tomorrow?
He spends money as if he **were** a millionaire.
She looked as though she **had seen** a ghost.
Supposing it **rained** tomorrow, would we still go?
Imagine you **lived** in the 18th century.
If only I **had** more time to travel!

mistakes.wrong: It's time we go home.
mistakes.right: It's time we went home. / It's time to go home.
mistakes.why: It's time + subject + past.

mistakes.wrong: I'd rather you don't smoke here.
mistakes.right: I'd rather you didn't smoke here.
mistakes.why: Different subject: would rather + past.

mistakes.wrong: I'd rather to stay at home.
mistakes.right: I'd rather stay at home.
mistakes.why: Same subject: would rather + base form, no to.

mistakes.wrong: It's about time you get a job.
mistakes.right: It's about time you got a job.
mistakes.why: It's about time + past.

mistakes.wrong: She looked as if she has seen a ghost.
mistakes.right: She looked as if she had seen a ghost.
mistakes.why: Unreal past: past perfect.

mistakes.wrong: I'd rather you didn't tell her yesterday.
mistakes.right: I'd rather you hadn't told her.
mistakes.why: For the past: would rather + past perfect.

items.prompt: It's late. It's time we ___ home.
I'd rather you ___ smoke in the house.
He talks as if he ___ everything, but he doesn't.
I'd rather ___ at home tonight. I'm tired.
items.explanation: Same subject: would rather + base form, **stay**.

items.prompt: Suppose you ___ a million dollars. What would you do?
It's high time the government ___ something about pollution.
She looked as though she ___ a ghost.
items.explanation: Unreal, earlier than *looked*: past perfect, **had seen**.

items.prompt: Would you rather I ___ you tomorrow?
Imagine you ___ in the 18th century. How would your life be different?
It's about time you ___ a job!
I'd rather we ___ about this now. Can we talk tomorrow?
items.explanation: Different subject: would rather + past, **didn't talk**.

items.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: It's time + subject + past: **It's time we left.**

items.prompt: He spends money as if he ___ a millionaire. (He isn't.)
My parents would rather I ___ medicine, not art.
Supposing it ___ tomorrow, would we still go?
If only I ___ more time to travel!
items.explanation: Unreal present wish: if only + past, **had**.

topics.h1: Probability: Bound To, May Well, Likely To
intro: Beyond *will, might* and *probably*, English has many ways to say **how likely** something is: *He's **bound to** call. It **may well** rain. Prices are **likely to** rise.*
These expressions help you sound more precise and natural, especially in writing and discussion.

rows: **be bound to**, **be sure to**, **be certain to**
She's **bound to** pass. She's so well prepared.
**be likely to**, **may / might / could well**, **there's a good chance (that)**, **in all likelihood**, **the chances are (that)**
**be unlikely to**, **it's doubtful whether**, **there's little chance (that)**

items: *bound / sure / certain / likely / unlikely* + **to + verb**: *He's **likely to** be late.* Or *It's likely **that** he'll be late.* (not *It's bound that*)
*may / might / could* + **well** + verb: *She **may well** be right.* (= it's quite likely)
*chance* + **that** clause: *There's a good chance **that** it'll rain.* *The chances **are** (that)…* (plural verb)
*probably / definitely*: after *will*, before *won't*: *He**'ll probably** forget. She **probably won't** come.*

blocks.md: *Bound to* often sounds like a confident prediction from experience: *It's **bound to** rain. It always rains on my birthday.*

items.text: Don't worry, he's **bound to** call you back.
With this traffic, we're **sure to** be late.
Prices are **likely to** rise again next year.
She **may well** be right, but we need more evidence.
There's **a good chance** that it'll snow this weekend.
**In all likelihood**, the project will be finished by May.
**The chances are** that he's forgotten.
The new rule is **unlikely to** make much difference.
It's **highly unlikely** that they'll win.
There's **no chance** that he'll change his mind.

mistakes.wrong: He's bound pass the exam.
mistakes.right: He's bound to pass the exam.
mistakes.why: Bound to + verb.

mistakes.wrong: It's bound that he will win.
mistakes.right: He's bound to win.
mistakes.why: Bound / sure don't take It… that.

mistakes.wrong: She may good be right.
mistakes.right: She may well be right.
mistakes.why: May / might / could well.

mistakes.wrong: He'll forget probably.
mistakes.right: He'll probably forget.
mistakes.why: Probably goes after will.

mistakes.wrong: The chances is that he'll be late.
mistakes.right: The chances are that he'll be late.
mistakes.why: The chances are (plural).

mistakes.wrong: It's very impossible.
mistakes.right: It's highly unlikely. / It's impossible.
mistakes.why: Impossible is already extreme; use highly with unlikely.

items.prompt: Don't worry, he's bound ___ call you back.
It's ___ that the meeting will be cancelled. The boss is ill.
items.explanation: It's **likely** that… (*bound* and *sure* don't take *It… that*).

items.prompt: She may ___ be right, but we need more evidence.
There's a good ___ that it will rain this afternoon.
The chances ___ that he'll be late again.
He'll ___ forget. He always does.
She probably ___ come to the party. She's very busy.
items.explanation: She's busy, so negative; *probably* goes before *won't*: probably **won't**.

items.prompt: Prices are ___ to rise again next year.
It's highly ___ that they'll win. They haven't won a game all season.
In all ___, the project will be finished by May.
Choose the correct sentence.
options: She's bound to passing the exam.
She bounds to pass the exam.
She's bound to pass the exam.

items.prompt: We could ___ see snow this weekend. The forecast says it's quite likely.
There's no ___ that he'll change his mind.
He's ___ to be late. The traffic is terrible.
The new rule is unlikely ___ much difference.
It ___ well rain later, so take an umbrella.

topics.h1: Future in the Past (was about to, was to, would)
intro: Sometimes we talk about the past and need to say what was **in the future at that time**: *I knew she **would** call. I **was about to** leave when the phone rang.*
You probably know *was going to*. This page covers the other forms: **would, was about to, was on the point of, was to** and **was to have done**.

rows: future seen from the past (prediction, promise, report)
He promised he **would** be back by midnight.
very near future at that time
I **was about to** leave when the phone rang.
even nearer; just about to (often interrupted)
She **was on the point of giving** up when she found the answer.
destiny (what really happened later), or an official plan
They met in 1990. They **were to** marry ten years later.
The meeting **was to have taken** place at 10, but it was cancelled.

blocks.md: *Would* is common after reporting and thinking verbs in the past: *I thought it **would** be a nice day. She said the package **would** arrive the next day. As a child, I had no idea that one day I **would** live in Canada.*
See [Reported Speech](/blog/grammar/reported-speech/) for *will → would* in reported statements.

*Was to* is often used in biographies and stories to say what happened later, seen from an earlier moment: *At the time, nobody knew that this small shop **was to** become a global brand.* It sounds literary, so it's mostly used in writing.
*Little did they know that…* often comes before *was to* or *would*: *Little did I know that the decision **was to** change my life.*

items.text: I knew he **would** never see her again.
We **were about to** have dinner when the guests arrived.
The train **was** just **about to** leave when we got to the platform.
He **was on the point of** resigning when they offered him a promotion.
She **was to** become one of the most famous writers of her time.
The new hospital **was to have been** opened in 2020, but the work was delayed.
I thought it **would** be easy, but it wasn't.
I couldn't believe what I **was about to** see.
The president **was to** visit the factory the next day.
At that moment, I didn't know the decision **was to** change my life.

mistakes.wrong: I was about leaving when you called.
mistakes.right: I was about to leave when you called.
mistakes.why: About to + base form.

mistakes.wrong: She was on the point to give up.
mistakes.right: She was on the point of giving up.
mistakes.why: On the point of + -ing.

mistakes.wrong: He said he will call me.
mistakes.right: He said he would call me.
mistakes.why: Future from a past point of view: would.

mistakes.wrong: They were to married in 2000.
mistakes.right: They were to marry in 2000.
mistakes.why: Was / were to + base form.

items.prompt: I was ___ to leave when the phone rang.
items.explanation: Very near future at that time: was **about** to.

items.prompt: She was on the point ___ up when she finally found the answer.
He knew he ___ never see her again.
They met in 1990. Little did they know that they ___ married ten years later.
The meeting ___ at 10, but it was cancelled.
items.explanation: A plan that didn't happen: **was to have taken place**.

items.prompt: We were about ___ dinner when the guests arrived.
I thought it ___ a nice day, but it rained all afternoon.
items.explanation: Future from a past point of view: **would be**.

items.prompt: She was ___ become one of the most famous writers of her time.
The train ___ leave when we got to the platform.
items.explanation: Very near future in the past: **was about to**.

items.prompt: He promised he ___ back by midnight.
items.explanation: A past promise about the future: **would be**.

items.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I was about leaving when you called.
I was on the point to leave when you called.
I was about to leaving when you called.
I was on the point of leaving when you called.

items.prompt: The new hospital was ___ opened in 2020, but the work was delayed.
items.explanation: A failed plan, passive: was **to have been** opened.

items.prompt: I couldn't believe what I ___ to see.
As a child, I had no idea that one day I ___ live in Canada.
At that moment, I didn't know that the decision ___ change my life.
She said the package ___ the next day.

intro: **Concession** means accepting one fact while saying something that contrasts with it. At B1 you learned *although, despite* and *in spite of*.
At C1, you can use more precise and formal forms: *The plan worked, **albeit** slowly. **Much as** I like him, I don't trust him. **Notwithstanding** the weather, the event went ahead.*

rows: an adjective, adverb or phrase (not a full clause)
It was a good, **albeit** short, holiday.
**Much as** I'd love to help, I don't have time.
a noun (before or after it); formal
**Notwithstanding** the cost, the plan was approved. / These problems **notwithstanding**, …
a clause (= it doesn't matter how)
**However hard** I try, I can't understand it.
**Strange as** it may seem, I've never seen the sea.

blocks.md: *Albeit* can't start a clause with a subject and verb: *albeit slowly* / *albeit with some problems* (not *albeit it was slow*).

*Although / though / even though* + clause; *despite / in spite of* + noun or -ing; *while / whilst* + clause for contrast. See [Although, Despite, In Spite Of](/blog/grammar/although-despite-in-spite-of/).

items.text: He accepted the offer, **albeit** reluctantly.
The results were positive, **albeit** with a few exceptions.
**Much as** I admire her work, I can't agree with her.
**Notwithstanding** the bad weather, the concert went ahead.
Budget limits **notwithstanding**, the team delivered on time.
**However much** you earn, you'll always want more.
**Tired though** she was, she kept working.
**Strange as** it may seem, I've never been on a plane.
The test was hard. **Nevertheless**, everyone passed.
**While** she's very talented, she's also very modest.

mistakes.wrong: Albeit it was cold, we went out.
mistakes.right: Although it was cold, we went out.
mistakes.why: Albeit doesn't take a subject + verb.

mistakes.wrong: Much as I like him, but I don't trust him.
mistakes.right: Much as I like him, I don't trust him.
mistakes.why: Don't add but after a concession clause.

mistakes.wrong: However I try hard, I can't do it.
mistakes.right: However hard I try, I can't do it.
mistakes.why: However + adjective / adverb comes first.

mistakes.wrong: Notwithstanding it rained, we played.
mistakes.right: Notwithstanding the rain, we played.
mistakes.why: Notwithstanding + noun.

mistakes.wrong: Strange as may it seem, it's true.
mistakes.right: Strange as it may seem, it's true.
mistakes.why: No inversion after as: subject + verb.

mistakes.wrong: Despite it was risky, we tried.
mistakes.right: Despite the risk, we tried. / Although it was risky, we tried.
mistakes.why: Despite + noun or -ing, not a clause.

items.prompt: The plan was successful, ___ expensive.
___ I like him, I don't trust him.
items.explanation: **Much as** + clause = although I like him very much.

items.prompt: ___ hard I try, I can't understand this.
___ the bad weather, the event went ahead.
Strange ___ it may seem, I've never seen the sea.
He accepted the offer, ___ reluctantly.
The results were disappointing. ___, we learned a lot.
Tired ___ she was, she kept working.
The project, ___ its high cost, was approved.
___ I'd love to help, I simply don't have time.
Choose the correct sentence.
options: Albeit it was cold, we went out.
It was a good, albeit short, holiday.
Albeit the rain, we enjoyed it.
We enjoyed it, albeit we were tired.

items.prompt: ___ much I admire her work, I can't agree with her.
___ the fact that he was ill, he went to work.
These problems ___, the launch was a success.
___ she's very talented, she's also very modest.
Much ___ I enjoy my job, I need a break.

intro: In English, a noun can describe another noun: *a **bus** stop, a **shoe** shop, a **coffee** cup.* The first noun works like an adjective, and the **second** noun is the main one: a *shoe shop* is a kind of shop.
Some combinations are written as one word (*toothbrush*), some as two (*bus stop*) and some with a hyphen (*a ten-minute walk*).

sections.h2: The first noun is usually singular

blocks.md: *a **shoe** shop* (not *shoes shop*), *a **toothbrush*** (not *teethbrush*), *a **taxi** driver*, *a **book** club*.
Some are plural by tradition: *a **sports** car, a **clothes** shop, a **savings** account, the **sales** department, a **goods** train*.

When a number + noun comes **before** another noun, use a hyphen and a singular noun: *a **ten-minute** walk, a **five-year-old** girl, a **five-star** hotel, a **million-dollar** budget, a **two-hour** meeting*.
Compare: *The walk takes ten **minutes**. She's five **years** old.* (not before a noun, so plural)

rows: a type of thing, its purpose or material
a **coffee cup** (a cup for coffee), a **glass door**, a **football match**
a container with its contents, or a part
a **cup of coffee** (a cup with coffee in it), the **end of the film**
possession by a person or animal

blocks.md: In speech, compound nouns usually have the **stress on the first part**: *BUS stop, TOOTHbrush, FOOTball match.*

items.text: Where's the nearest **bus stop**?
Put the plates in the **dishwasher**.
It's a **ten-minute walk** from here.
They have a **five-year-old** son.
We stayed in a **five-star hotel**.
He drives a **sports car**.
I need to open a **savings account**.
Could I have a **glass of water**?
The **football match** was cancelled.
Our **team meeting** is at 9.

mistakes.wrong: She works in a shoes shop.
mistakes.right: She works in a shoe shop.
mistakes.why: The first noun is usually singular.

mistakes.wrong: It's a ten-minutes walk.
mistakes.right: It's a ten-minute walk.
mistakes.why: Number + noun before a noun: singular, with a hyphen.

mistakes.wrong: My son is a five-years-old boy.
mistakes.right: My son is a five-year-old boy.
mistakes.why: No -s in a compound before a noun.

mistakes.wrong: I'd like a coffee cup, please. (You want to drink coffee.)
mistakes.right: I'd like a cup of coffee, please.
mistakes.why: Cup of coffee = a cup with coffee in it.

mistakes.wrong: He drives a sport car.
mistakes.right: He drives a sports car.
mistakes.why: Fixed compound: sports car.

mistakes.wrong: The stop of the bus is there.
mistakes.right: The bus stop is there.
mistakes.why: Use the compound noun.

items.prompt: It's a ___ walk from here to the station.
items.explanation: Number + noun before a noun: **ten-minute** (singular, hyphen).

items.prompt: My daughter is a ___ girl.
Where's the nearest ___?
Could I have a ___, please? I'm really thirsty.
items.explanation: A glass with water in it: **glass of water**.

items.prompt: Put the dirty plates in the ___.
She works in a ___.
He drives a red ___.
items.explanation: Fixed compound with a plural first noun: **sports car**.

items.prompt: I need to open a ___ account.
Can you pass me that ___? I want to pour some tea.
items.explanation: You pour from a **teapot** (a pot for tea).
